request.questionText: The grocery.csv file contains pricing data on 40 different products collected from 16 different Texas stores. Variables include in this data frame include: category: type of product (Cereal, Drink, Fruit, Snack, Spread/Sauce, Staple) city: store location (Austin, Fort Worth, Houston) income: average income in ZIP code where the store is located, in dollars population: population in ZIP code where the store is located price: cost of product, in dollars product: one of 40 grocery products appearing in various sample stores. (baseline category: "12 Pack DrPepper") type: type of store (Convenience, Grocery, High-end Grocery, Natural, Small Format) A prevalent social policy problem in many communities, "food deserts" describe urban, low-income areas that are under-served by grocery stores selling affordable quality fresh food. In a food desert, the best option for groceries might be a convenience store, rather than a full-service grocery store. If convenience stores charge more for the same product (perhaps due to lack of scale) under-privileged citizens might end up paying more for food than others living in more affluent areas. Do consumers in lower-income ZIP codes pay more or less for groceries? You decide to fit a regression model to investigate this phenomenon. To facilitate interpretation of the model, first add to the data frame a new column called income10k to record the income variable in units of ten-thousand (10000) dollars. Then, fit a model to predict price in terms of two predictors: (1) income10k and (2) product. Use large-sample inference to generate confidence intervals. Fill in each blank below with the best answer based on results of this model: The [ Select ] ["positive", "negative"] sign of the income10k coefficient suggests that consumers in lower-income ZIP codes pay [ Select ] ["more", "less"] on average for the same product. The 95% confidence interval for income10k suggests that (when comparing prices for the same product) an increase of $10000 is associated with a decrease of at most approximately [ Select ] ["1/2 cent", "3 cents", "2 cents", "1 cent"] in price. Because the confidence interval for income10k [ Select ] ["does not include zero", "includes zero"] we may conclude that this [ Select ] ["overall relationship", "partial relationship"] is [ Select ] ["not statistically significant", "statistically significant"] . This model estimates [ Select ] ["the same slope", "different slopes"] for the relationship between price and income10k across product categories.
